outcome: In August 2024, Ryan Propper (working within the PrimeGrid distributed-computing project) found that 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1 is prime, eliminating k = 107347 as a candidate for a Riesel number smaller than 509,203. This is a case-elimination on the exact problem stated (whether 509,203 is the lowest Riesel number), reducing the pool of unresolved k values below 509,203 from 42 to 41. The conjecture that 509,203 is the smallest Riesel number remains open, and multiple sources confirm the count has stayed at 41 as of mid-2026, indicating no further eliminations occurred in the window.

counterexample.object: 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1, a 7,052,391-digit prime, showing k = 107347 is not a Riesel number and thus cannot be a counterexample to '509,203 is the lowest Riesel number' (it removes a candidate rather than exhibiting one)
counterexample.verified_how: Primality proved by Lucas–Lehmer–Riesel (LLR) test, standard for numbers of this form; distributed/verified through the PrimeGrid project infrastructure

summary: The problem asks whether 509,203 is the lowest Riesel number (a k such that k·2^n − 1 is composite for all n ≥ 1). As of the frozen Wikipedia revision (26 Jan 2024), the list of candidate k values below 509,203 not yet ruled out stood at 42 (57 of the original 101 candidates had been eliminated by finding a prime k·2^n − 1 for that k, as of December 2022, with no elimination recorded between then and the freeze date). In August 2024, Ryan Propper — working within PrimeGrid, the distributed-computing project that coordinates this search — found 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1 to be prime, which is a 7,052,391-digit number. This eliminates k = 107347 from the candidate pool, since finding any prime of the form k·2^n − 1 proves k is not a Riesel number. This is squarely a case-elimination on the stated problem (§3.1): finding one more prime among the remaining candidates directly shrinks the set of numbers that could be a smaller Riesel number than 509,203, which is exactly what the bullet asks about. I classify this as 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (the elimination is consistent with, and narrows in on, the conjecture that 509,203 is indeed the smallest). The list of 41 remaining unresolved k values (23669, 31859, 38473, 46663, 67117, 74699, 81041, 121889, 129007, 143047, 161669, 206231, 215443, 226153, 234343, 245561, 250027, 315929, 319511, 324011, 325123, 327671, 336839, 342847, 344759, 362609, 363343, 364903, 365159, 368411, 371893, 384539, 386801, 397027, 409753, 444637, 470173, 474491, 477583, 485557, 494743) has been reported consistently across sources from November 2024 through at least July 2026 (one search result cites 'as of July 29, 2026, there remain 41 uncertain candidates, and the coordinated search has currently reached n < 16984600'), which corroborates that no further eliminations occurred after the August 2024 one within this window — the underlying search (PrimeGrid's 'The Riesel Problem' subproject) has continued extending the tested range of n for the remaining k values without producing a new prime. On AI: this is a distributed-computing / GPU sieving and primality-testing effort (LLR/PRP testing, standard number-theoretic algorithms), and no source — Wikipedia's live article, PrimeGrid's project pages, or general search results on Propper's methods — mentions any AI or machine-learning system contributing to the search, sieving, or verification. Propper's other prime discoveries (Proth primes, etc.) are likewise attributed to conventional primality-testing software (LLR) run on CPU/GPU hardware. I therefore set ai_role to none.
competing_reading: One could argue the conjecture ('509,203 is the lowest Riesel number') is only truly settled when it is proven — i.e., when all 41 remaining candidates are eliminated or a smaller Riesel number is found — and that a single elimination is too incremental to register as anything beyond background progress on an open problem, arguably better captured as 'progress' rather than 'partial'. However, per §3.1, a case of the problem (here, one specific k value being ruled out) counts as 'partial' regardless of size, since it changes what a careful person would write about which k values remain live candidates for beating 509,203. I have followed that instruction literally.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (via exhaustive search or covering-set argument) that all 41 remaining k values are eliminated, or discovery of a Riesel number smaller than 509,203, would resolve the conjecture. Absent that, any future PrimeGrid/Propper/other announcement of a prime k·2^n − 1 for one of the 41 remaining k values would be a further 'partial' event to record separately.
